endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Lastly, some vendors will not voluntarily commit to advance notification of model/solution updates or feature changes: in those cases, HDOs should consider adding periodic feature-inventory audits and/or contractual notification requirements as compensating controls.

commentary.bottom_line: No study supplied tests whether periodic feature-inventory audits detect undisclosed AI changes in health IT systems, and no study documents how often such changes occur. The recommendation rests on one governance framework that presents these audits as a compensating control when vendors decline to give advance notice.

perspectives.view: The evidence base for this recommendation contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The single support is expert consensus from one framework, which GRADE methodologists would not treat as evidence of effect.

The CHAI playbook uses permissive language, stating that health systems should consider feature-inventory audits and/or contractual notification requirements. It frames audits as one of two compensating controls rather than a required step. A health system could satisfy the guidance through contract terms alone, and the framework carries no regulatory force.

commentary.research_gap: No study measures how often vendors introduce AI features or model updates without notice, whether periodic feature-inventory audits find those changes, how quickly they find them, or what the audits cost in staff time. Studies comparing audits with contractual notification clauses would help health systems choose between the two controls the framework names.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice in any population, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. Safety-net systems may have less staff capacity to run audits and less bargaining power to negotiate notification clauses, but the supplied evidence does not address this.
